summary: In our project, we studied how fire behaves in microgravity using science. Using data and measurements, we developed a project that analyses microgravity combustion data to understand why flame in space acts differently compared to Earth. By studying factors such as flame shape, temperature and burning behaviour. Our project manages the challenge by turning scientific information into useful insights that can help people understand and prevent fire hazards. This is important, because fire in space can be extremely dangerous, as flames behaves differently. Our research can help improve astronaut safety and contribute to better fire prevention on our planet Earth.
details:
Our web dashboard acts as an AI-powered fire safety assistant that makes NASA’s microgravity combustion research easy to search, compare, and understand. Users can select a specific mission environment—such as the International Space Station, a lunar habitat, or a Mars spacecraft—and instantly see which NASA experiments are most relevant, complete with plain-English summaries, fire risk rankings, and key measurements like oxygen levels, airflow speed, and material flammability.

To build the tool, we gathered experimental parameters and findings from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database and official ISS research reports, including landmark studies like BASS-II, FLEX, Saffire, and SoFIE. We organized this data into an interactive interface powered by AI synthesis, allowing engineers and students to compare flame behavior in zero and partial gravity, identify hardware guidelines for better smoke detectors and fire extinguishers, and explore how these space discoveries improve fire safety on Earth.

As NASA prepares for long-duration human missions to the Moon and Mars where higher oxygen levels and lower gravity increase fire risks, our platform saves valuable research time by turning complex technical archives into clear, actionable safety insights.
dataRefs: • NASA PSI Dataset Identifiers: PSI-1042, PSI-0832, PSI-1203, PSI-1188, and PSI-1214. • BASS-II (Burning and Suppression of Solids): Cited for its Limiting Oxygen Concentration (LOC) threshold of 15.2% O₂. • Saffire-II & Saffire-V (Spacecraft Fire Experiment): Cited for the 2.8× vs 1g flame velocity multiplier at 34% O₂ and 56.5 kPa, as well as Nomex/silicon-coated barrier validations. • SoFIE-MIST (Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction): Cited for empirical trial limits (36.5% O₂ and 22 cm/s crossflow) and 25 µm water-mist kinetics. • FLEX-2 (Flame Extinguishment Experiment): Cited for microgravity soot-precursor spectra used in Earth battery-vault smoke detection.
